disease.name: Hyperthyroidism

overview.description: Hyperthyroidism is a condition in which the thyroid gland is overactive and produces excessive amounts of thyroid hormones (thyroxine/T4 and triiodothyronine/T3). This accelerates the body's metabolism, causing rapid heartbeat, unintended weight loss, increased appetite, heat intolerance, anxiety, and tremors. It is the most common thyroid disorder after hypothyroidism and requires timely diagnosis and management to prevent life-threatening complications.
overview.affected_organ: Thyroid Gland (and secondarily: Heart, Bones, Eyes, Nervous System)
overview.prevalence: Affects approximately 1.2% of the US population; 0.5-1% globally; Graves' disease accounts for 70-80% of all cases.
overview.age_group: Mainly adults aged 20-50; women are 5-10 times more likely to develop hyperthyroidism than men.

types.name: Graves' Disease
types.description: The most common cause of hyperthyroidism (~70-80%). An autoimmune disorder where the immune system produces TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb/TSI) that continuously stimulate the thyroid gland to produce excess hormones. It is the only form of hyperthyroidism associated with eye disease (Graves' ophthalmopathy) and pretibial myxedema.
types.common_in: Women aged 20-40; strong genetic and autoimmune component

types.name: Toxic Multinodular Goiter (Plummer's Disease)
types.description: Multiple thyroid nodules develop over years and become autonomous — producing thyroid hormones independently of TSH regulation. Second most common cause of hyperthyroidism.
types.common_in: Older adults (>50 years), particularly in iodine-deficient areas

types.name: Toxic Adenoma (Single Hot Nodule)
types.description: A single benign thyroid nodule (adenoma) that autonomously secretes excessive thyroid hormone, suppressing TSH and suppressing the rest of the thyroid gland.
types.common_in: Adults; palpable solitary thyroid nodule on examination

types.name: Subacute (De Quervain's) Thyroiditis
types.description: Inflammation of the thyroid gland, often following a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Stored thyroid hormones leak into the blood causing a transient hyperthyroid phase (2-6 weeks), followed by hypothyroidism, then recovery.
types.common_in: Women aged 20-50; often following viral illness (mumps, influenza, COVID-19)

types.name: Postpartum Thyroiditis
types.description: Transient autoimmune thyroid inflammation occurring within 1 year of childbirth. Follows a classic pattern: hyperthyroid phase (1-4 months postpartum), hypothyroid phase, then recovery. Recurs in subsequent pregnancies.
types.common_in: Women within 12 months of delivery; affects 5-9% of postpartum women

types.name: Iodine-Induced Hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow Effect)
types.description: Excessive iodine exposure (from amiodarone, contrast dye, kelp/seaweed supplements, or iodine-rich diets) triggers overproduction of thyroid hormones in individuals with pre-existing nodular goiter or latent Graves' disease.
types.common_in: Patients receiving amiodarone, contrast dye, or high iodine supplements

types.name: Factitious (Exogenous) Thyrotoxicosis
types.description: Hyperthyroidism caused by intentional or accidental intake of excessive exogenous thyroid hormone (levothyroxine). Thyroglobulin levels are low; no goiter present.
types.common_in: Patients on thyroid medication who take excessive doses; healthcare workers

types.name: TSH-Secreting Pituitary Adenoma
types.description: A rare benign tumor of the pituitary gland that produces excess TSH, which continuously stimulates the thyroid gland. TSH is inappropriately normal or elevated despite high T3/T4.
types.common_in: Rare; any adult; usually presents with visual symptoms from pituitary mass

types.name: Gestational Transient Thyrotoxicosis
types.description: Mild, transient hyperthyroidism occurring in the first trimester of pregnancy due to the thyroid-stimulating effect of high hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) levels. Associated with hyperemesis gravidarum.
types.common_in: First trimester of pregnancy; women with severe morning sickness

severity_levels.name: Subclinical Hyperthyroidism
severity_levels.description: Mildest form; no or very mild symptoms
severity_levels.lab_values: TSH < 0.4 mIU/L; Free T3 and Free T4 within normal range
severity_levels.impact: Increased risk of atrial fibrillation and bone density loss over time; clinical monitoring required
severity_levels.management: Watchful waiting or low-dose antithyroid therapy depending on age and cardiovascular risk

severity_levels.name: Overt (Mild to Moderate) Hyperthyroidism
severity_levels.description: Noticeable symptoms affecting quality of life
severity_levels.lab_values: TSH < 0.1 mIU/L; Free T4 and/or Free T3 elevated above normal range
severity_levels.impact: Palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance, tremors, anxiety, sweating; requires active treatment
severity_levels.management: Antithyroid drugs (methimazole or PTU) as first-line; beta-blockers for symptom relief; definitive treatment considered

severity_levels.name: Severe Hyperthyroidism
severity_levels.description: Significant thyroid hormone excess with multi-system involvement
severity_levels.lab_values: TSH undetectable; markedly elevated Free T4 and Free T3
severity_levels.impact: Atrial fibrillation, heart failure, severe osteoporosis, psychiatric disturbances; high urgency
severity_levels.management: Aggressive antithyroid therapy; beta-blockers; definitive treatment (RAI or surgery) urgently planned

severity_levels.name: Thyroid Storm (Thyrotoxic Crisis)
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism; medical emergency with multi-organ failure
severity_levels.lab_values: Markedly elevated Free T3 and Free T4; Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale score ≥45 is diagnostic
severity_levels.impact: High fever (>38.5°C), extreme tachycardia (>140 bpm), agitation, delirium, heart failure, coma; mortality 10-30% even with treatment
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; IV propylthiouracil or methimazole; Lugol's iodine; beta-blockers IV; steroids; active cooling; treat precipitant

genetic_factors: Family history of thyroid disorders or autoimmune diseases (Graves', Hashimoto's)
Associated HLA genes: HLA-DR3 and HLA-B8 in Caucasians; CTLA4, PTPN22, CD25 gene variants
Personal history of other autoimmune conditions (Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, Addison's disease)
Female sex — strong genetic predisposition; 5-10x more common in women
environmental_triggers: Excessive iodine intake through diet (seaweed, kelp), supplements, or medications (amiodarone, iodine contrast dye)
Stressful major life events (bereavement, surgery, severe illness) — may trigger Graves' disease onset
Pregnancy and postpartum period — hormonal and immune changes
Viral or bacterial infections (may trigger thyroiditis: influenza, mumps, COVID-19, Epstein-Barr virus)
Smoking — significantly increases risk of Graves' ophthalmopathy; independently increases Graves' disease risk
High-dose interferon-alpha or interleukin-2 therapy (immunotherapy-induced thyroiditis)
Checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy (e.g., pembrolizumab, nivolumab) — causes immune thyroiditis
other_causes: Amiodarone medication (contains 37% iodine by weight; causes both hypo- and hyperthyroidism)
Excessive exogenous thyroid hormone intake (levothyroxine over-medication or factitious use)
TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (rare — TSH inappropriately elevated despite high T4/T3)
Struma ovarii (rare ovarian teratoma containing functional thyroid tissue)
Hydatidiform mole or choriocarcinoma (hCG-mediated stimulation — very high hCG mimics TSH)
Metastatic follicular thyroid cancer producing thyroid hormones (rare)

primary_symptoms.name: Unexplained Weight Loss
primary_symptoms.description: Significant and unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite and food intake. Caused by hypermetabolism — accelerated basal metabolic rate from excess thyroid hormones.

primary_symptoms.name: Rapid Heart Rate (Tachycardia) and Palpitations
primary_symptoms.description: Resting heart rate consistently >100 bpm; sensation of pounding, racing, or irregular heartbeat. Thyroid hormones directly increase cardiac output and heart rate. Atrial fibrillation can develop.
primary_symptoms.onset: Constant or episodic; often noticed at rest

primary_symptoms.name: Heat Intolerance and Excessive Sweating
primary_symptoms.description: Feeling excessively warm even in cool environments; sweating more than normal (hyperhidrosis). Caused by increased metabolic rate producing excess body heat.

primary_symptoms.name: Fine Tremor of Hands and Fingers
primary_symptoms.description: Fine, rapid trembling of the outstretched hands and fingers. Caused by increased adrenergic stimulation of neuromuscular function.

primary_symptoms.name: Anxiety, Irritability, and Nervousness
primary_symptoms.description: Persistent anxiety, emotional lability, restlessness, irritability, and difficulty concentrating. Thyroid hormones amplify sympathetic nervous system activity.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual; may be mistaken for a psychiatric disorder

primary_symptoms.name: Goiter (Enlarged Thyroid Gland)
primary_symptoms.description: Visible or palpable swelling at the base of the neck. In Graves' disease, the goiter is diffuse and may have a bruit on auscultation. In toxic nodular goiter, the swelling is irregular and nodular.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual enlargement over months to years

primary_symptoms.name: Graves' Ophthalmopathy (Thyroid Eye Disease)
primary_symptoms.description: Specific to Graves' disease. Immune-mediated inflammation and swelling of orbital tissues causing proptosis (bulging eyes/exophthalmos), lid retraction, double vision, eye pain, light sensitivity, and potentially vision loss. Occurs in ~25-50% of Graves' disease patients.
primary_symptoms.onset: May precede, accompany, or follow hyperthyroidism diagnosis

secondary_symptoms: Fatigue and muscle weakness — especially proximal muscles (thighs, upper arms); difficulty climbing stairs
More frequent bowel movements or diarrhea
Increased appetite (polyphagia) — eating more yet losing weight
Decreased menstrual flow (oligomenorrhea) or absent periods (amenorrhea) in women
Reduced libido and erectile dysfunction in men
Fine, thin, or brittle hair; hair loss (telogen effluvium)
Thin, warm, and moist skin; onycholysis (nail separation from nail bed)
Pretibial myxedema (waxy, thickened skin on shins — specific to Graves' disease, rare)
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis (sudden muscle weakness — especially in Asian men with Graves' disease)
Shortened attention span and poor concentration
warning_signs_of_attack: High fever above 38.5°C (101.3°F) — especially with dehydration
Extreme rapid heartbeat >140 bpm or new onset atrial fibrillation
Agitation, confusion, delirium, psychosis, or hallucinations
Severe nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or diarrhea
Shortness of breath, chest pain, or signs of heart failure
Jaundice (yellowing of skin/eyes — rare; indicates liver involvement)
Profuse sweating with inability to tolerate heat
symptoms_in_children: Rapid linear growth and accelerated bone maturation (advanced bone age)
Behavioral problems — hyperactivity, short attention span, declining school performance
Increased appetite with failure to gain weight or weight loss
Emotional instability, anxiety, and sleep disturbances
Diffuse goiter — smooth, soft, symmetrical neck swelling
Tachycardia at rest and during sleep — characteristic finding
graves_specific_features: Graves' Ophthalmopathy (Thyroid Eye Disease / TED): proptosis, lid retraction, chemosis, diplopia
Pretibial Myxedema: waxy, non-pitting thickening of skin on shins and dorsum of feet
Thyroid Acropachy: rare triad of clubbing of fingers, periosteal new bone formation, and pretibial myxedema
Thyroid bruit: audible sound over the thyroid due to increased vascularity

medical_history: Family history of thyroid disorders, autoimmune diseases, or thyroid cancer
Current medications — especially amiodarone, lithium, interferon, checkpoint inhibitors, thyroid supplements
Recent iodine exposure — contrast dye, kelp supplements, iodine-containing antiseptics
History of pregnancy, postpartum period, or recent viral illness
Onset, duration, and progression of symptoms
Prior thyroid conditions, surgery, or radioactive iodine treatment
physical_examination: Palpation of the thyroid gland — size, texture, consistency, presence of nodules, and tenderness
Auscultation of the thyroid — bruit (vascular hum) present in Graves' disease due to high vascularity
Heart rate and rhythm assessment — resting tachycardia, irregular pulse (atrial fibrillation)
Blood pressure measurement — wide pulse pressure (high systolic, low diastolic) typical
Assessment of hand tremors — fine rapid tremor on outstretched hands
Eye examination — proptosis, lid lag, lid retraction, exophthalmos (Graves' ophthalmopathy)
Skin examination — warm, moist skin; pretibial myxedema; onycholysis
Proximal muscle strength testing — difficulty rising from squatting position

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures pituitary TSH levels. TSH is the most sensitive first-line screening test for thyroid dysfunction. In hyperthyroidism, excess thyroid hormones suppress TSH production via negative feedback.
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TSH < 0.4 mIU/L: subclinical; TSH < 0.1 mIU/L: overt hyperthyroidism; TSH undetectable (<0.01): severe

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures unbound (biologically active) thyroxine. Elevated in overt hyperthyroidism. Normal in subclinical hyperthyroidism.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirms overt hyperthyroidism and assesses severity
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal range: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL; Elevated (>1.8 ng/dL) in overt hyperthyroidism

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures unbound T3, the most biologically active thyroid hormone. In T3 thyrotoxicosis, T3 is elevated while T4 may be normal.
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal range: 2.3-4.1 pg/mL; Elevated (>4.4 pg/mL) in overt hyperthyroidism

diagnostic_tests.test_name: TSHR Antibody Test (TRAb / TSI — Thyroid Stimulating Immunoglobulin)
diagnostic_tests.description: Measures autoantibodies against the TSH receptor. Positive in Graves' disease. Used to confirm autoimmune hyperthyroidism and predict relapse after antithyroid drug treatment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirms Graves' disease; monitors treatment response; assesses risk of fetal/neonatal Graves'
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: TRAb > 1.75 IU/L (positive); TSI > 140% stimulation (positive) — confirms Graves' disease

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated in Hashimoto's thyroiditis and Graves' disease. Indicates autoimmune thyroid disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Supports diagnosis of autoimmune thyroid disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive (>35 IU/mL) in most Graves' disease and Hashimoto's patients

diagnostic_tests.description: Patient swallows a small dose of radioactive iodine (I-123 or I-131). Thyroid uptake measured at 4 and 24 hours using gamma camera. Iodine is selectively taken up by the thyroid gland.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Differentiates cause of hyperthyroidism — essential when etiology is unclear
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: High uptake (>35% at 24h): Graves' disease or toxic nodular goiter; Low/absent uptake (<5%): thyroiditis, factitious, or iodine excess

diagnostic_tests.description: Nuclear imaging using I-123 or technetium-99m pertechnetate. Shows distribution of thyroid activity — diffuse uptake in Graves'; focal hot spots in toxic nodular goiter or toxic adenoma.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identifies pattern and distribution of thyroid overactivity; guides RAI therapy dosing
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Diffuse uptake = Graves'; Single hot nodule = toxic adenoma; Multiple hot nodules = toxic multinodular goiter

diagnostic_tests.description: High-resolution ultrasound imaging of the thyroid gland. Doppler mode assesses vascularity. Detects nodules, goiter size, and calcifications.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detects thyroid nodules and goiter; assesses vascularity; guides fine-needle aspiration
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Increased diffuse vascularity ('thyroid inferno') in Graves'; discrete nodules in toxic nodular goiter; normal or absent vascularity in thyroiditis

diagnostic_tests.description: Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration of suspicious thyroid nodules. Cytological analysis of aspirated cells.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Excludes thyroid cancer in suspicious cold or solitary nodules
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bethesda system cytological classification (I-VI); not routinely done for hot nodules (low cancer risk)

diagnostic_tests.description: Records electrical activity of the heart. Detects arrhythmias associated with hyperthyroidism.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detects sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, or other arrhythmias
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Sinus tachycardia most common; atrial fibrillation in 10-15% of overt hyperthyroid patients

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures bone mineral density at lumbar spine and hip.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detects osteopenia or osteoporosis caused by chronic hyperthyroidism

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Complete Blood Count (CBC) and Liver Function Tests
diagnostic_tests.description: Baseline blood tests before starting antithyroid drugs. Agranulocytosis (rare but serious) and liver toxicity are potential side effects of methimazole and PTU.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Establishes baseline before antithyroid therapy; detects pre-existing abnormalities
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Monitor WBC and neutrophils; liver enzymes (ALT, AST, ALP, bilirubin)

medicines.note: All medications must be taken only under the supervision of a licensed physician or endocrinologist. Self-medication with thyroid medications is dangerous. Regular follow-up and blood tests are essential.

categories.purpose: Block thyroid peroxidase enzyme, inhibiting synthesis of new thyroid hormones (T3 and T4)
categories.onset: Clinical improvement within 2-6 weeks; TSH normalizes within 4-8 weeks
categories.duration: Typically 12-18 months for Graves' disease; 40-50% achieve long-term remission after course

medicines.name: Methimazole (MMI)
medicines.dosage: Mild: 5-10 mg/day; Moderate: 10-30 mg/day; Severe: 40-60 mg/day (in divided doses); maintenance 5-10 mg/day
medicines.use_case: First-line treatment for Graves' disease (except first trimester of pregnancy); toxic nodular goiter; toxic adenoma; pre-operative preparation
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase (TPO), blocking organification of iodine and coupling of thyroglobulin
side_effects: Agranulocytosis (0.1-0.5% — rare but life-threatening; neutrophil count <500/µL)
medicines.monitoring: CBC before starting; recheck if fever or sore throat develops (agranulocytosis warning); LFTs periodically; TSH/Free T4 every 4-8 weeks
medicines.warnings: Stop immediately and seek care if fever, sore throat, or mouth ulcers develop (possible agranulocytosis); avoid in first trimester pregnancy

medicines.name: Propylthiouracil (PTU)
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mg every 8 hours (total 300-600 mg/day) for severe disease; reduce to 50-100 mg two-three times daily for maintenance
medicines.use_case: Preferred in first trimester of pregnancy (safer for fetus than methimazole); thyroid storm (blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion); when methimazole not tolerated
medicines.mechanism: Inhibits TPO AND blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to more active T3 (additional advantage in thyroid storm)
side_effects: Fulminant hepatic necrosis — serious black box warning (0.1-0.2%)
medicines.monitoring: LFTs baseline and periodically — stop immediately if symptoms of liver damage (jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain); CBC monitoring
medicines.warnings: Black box warning for severe liver failure; use only when methimazole cannot be used; do NOT use in second/third trimester due to teratogenicity risk

categories.purpose: Block adrenergic (sympathetic) effects of excess thyroid hormones. Relieve palpitations, tachycardia, tremors, anxiety, and heat intolerance WITHOUT affecting thyroid hormone levels.
categories.duration: Used temporarily alongside antithyroid drugs until thyroid function normalizes; may be discontinued in 2-6 weeks

medicines.name: Propranolol
medicines.dosage: 10-40 mg three to four times daily (oral); 0.5-1 mg IV slowly (thyroid storm ICU setting)
medicines.use_case: Preferred beta-blocker for hyperthyroidism — also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion at high doses; used in thyroid storm
side_effects: Worsens heart failure in some patients
contraindications: Asthma or COPD (use selective beta-blockers instead)

medicines.name: Atenolol
medicines.use_case: Cardioselective (beta-1 selective); once-daily dosing improves adherence; preferred if mild respiratory concerns

medicines.name: Metoprolol Succinate
medicines.use_case: Cardioselective; extended release for once-daily dosing; good option for patients with borderline respiratory disease

medicines.name: Nadolol
medicines.use_case: Non-selective beta-blocker; long duration of action; used in hyperthyroidism management

categories.purpose: Selectively destroys thyroid cells by emitting beta radiation, permanently reducing thyroid size and hormone production. First-line definitive treatment in USA; used after antithyroid drug stabilization.
categories.note: Causes permanent hypothyroidism in 80-90% of patients within 6-12 months, requiring lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and moderate-severe Graves' ophthalmopathy.

medicines.name: Sodium Iodide I-131 (Radioiodine)
medicines.dosage: Single calculated dose based on thyroid size and RAIU: typically 10-15 mCi for Graves'; 20-30 mCi for toxic multinodular goiter
medicines.use_case: Definitive treatment for Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goiter, and toxic adenoma; adults who relapse after antithyroid drugs; patients not suitable for surgery
side_effects: Temporary worsening of hyperthyroid symptoms in first 2 weeks
Permanent hypothyroidism (expected and managed with levothyroxine)
Worsening of Graves' ophthalmopathy (pretreat with steroids if eye disease present)
medicines.post_treatment: TSH should be checked at 4-6 weeks, then monthly until stable; start levothyroxine when hypothyroid; lifelong thyroid function monitoring

categories.category_name: Iodine Solutions — Acute Pre-Surgical and Thyroid Storm Management
categories.purpose: High-dose iodine paradoxically blocks thyroid hormone release (Wolff-Chaikoff effect) and reduces thyroid vascularity. Used to prepare for surgery or in thyroid storm — always given AFTER antithyroid drugs.
categories.note: Must be given 1 hour AFTER antithyroid drugs to prevent organification of iodine into new thyroid hormone

medicines.name: Lugol's Iodine Solution
medicines.dosage: 3-5 drops (0.1-0.3 mL) three times daily for 10 days pre-operatively; in thyroid storm: 5-10 drops every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Pre-operative preparation for thyroidectomy (reduces vascularity and bleeding); thyroid storm treatment (second agent, given 1 hour after PTU/methimazole)
side_effects: Iodism (headache, runny nose, salivary gland swelling with prolonged use)

medicines.name: Potassium Iodide (SSKI)
medicines.dosage: 250 mg (5 drops of SSKI) every 6 hours in thyroid storm
medicines.use_case: Thyroid storm management; pre-operative preparation; radiation emergencies to protect thyroid

categories.category_name: Corticosteroids — Thyroid Storm and Graves' Ophthalmopathy
categories.purpose: Reduce inflammation; block peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion (dexamethasone); treat Graves' ophthalmopathy; adjunct in thyroid storm

medicines.name: Dexamethasone
medicines.dosage: 2 mg every 6 hours IV (thyroid storm); 0.5-2 mg daily (Graves' ophthalmopathy adjunct)
medicines.use_case: Thyroid storm — blocks T4-to-T3 conversion, reduces inflammation, treats possible adrenal insufficiency; Graves' ophthalmopathy

medicines.name: Methylprednisolone (IV Pulse)
medicines.dosage: 500 mg IV once weekly for 6 weeks, then 250 mg IV once weekly for 6 weeks (European EUGOGO protocol for Graves' ophthalmopathy)
medicines.use_case: Moderate-severe active Graves' ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease/TED)

categories.purpose: Definitive surgical treatment. Removes part or all of the thyroid gland. Preferred when RAI is contraindicated, when very large goiter causes compression, or when thyroid cancer coexists.
categories.note: Requires pre-operative preparation with antithyroid drugs and beta-blockers to achieve euthyroid state to reduce surgical risk

medicines.name: Total Thyroidectomy
medicines.use_case: Severe Graves' disease; large compressive goiter; coexisting thyroid nodule suspicious for cancer; patient preference; pregnancy when drugs not tolerated in second trimester
medicines.pre_op_preparation: Methimazole or PTU for 6-8 weeks to achieve euthyroid state; beta-blockers; Lugol's iodine 10 days pre-op to reduce vascularity

medicines.name: Subtotal Thyroidectomy
medicines.use_case: Toxic multinodular goiter; toxic adenoma; preserves small remnant of thyroid tissue
medicines.note: Higher relapse rate of hyperthyroidism compared to total thyroidectomy; rarely performed now

categories.purpose: After RAI or thyroidectomy, patients typically develop permanent hypothyroidism requiring lifelong thyroid hormone replacement to maintain normal metabolism.

medicines.name: Levothyroxine Sodium (L-T4)
medicines.dosage: 1.6 mcg/kg/day as starting dose; titrate to maintain TSH in normal range (0.5-4.0 mIU/L); dose range typically 50-200 mcg/day
medicines.use_case: Lifelong thyroid hormone replacement after RAI or thyroidectomy; post-ablative hypothyroidism; treatment of hypothyroidism developing spontaneously
side_effects: None at correct dose; overdose causes iatrogenic hyperthyroidism
Bone density loss if TSH suppressed long-term
medicines.administration: Take on empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast; avoid calcium, iron supplements, antacids within 4 hours; consistent timing essential
medicines.monitoring: TSH every 6-8 weeks after dose change; annually once stable; symptoms of both hypo- and hyperthyroidism

categories.purpose: Hyperthyroidism accelerates bone resorption causing osteopenia and osteoporosis. Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation is essential in all hyperthyroid patients.

medicines.name: Calcium Carbonate / Calcium Citrate
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg daily (calcium carbonate with food; calcium citrate fasting)
medicines.use_case: Prevent and treat hyperthyroidism-related bone loss; post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism

medicines.name: Cholecalciferol (Vitamin D3)
medicines.dosage: 1000-2000 IU daily (maintenance); 60,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks if deficient (as per Indian guidelines)
medicines.use_case: Vitamin D supplementation in all hyperthyroid patients with bone density concern; post-hypoparathyroidism
side_effects: Hypercalcemia with excessive doses (rare at recommended doses)

medicines.name: Bisphosphonates (e.g., Alendronate)
medicines.use_case: Established osteoporosis due to chronic hyperthyroidism; T-score < -2.5 on DEXA scan
side_effects: Atypical femoral fracture (rare with long-term use)

categories.purpose: Treat autoimmune inflammatory eye disease in Graves' disease. Severity-based treatment from supportive to immunosuppressive to surgical.

medicines.name: Teprotumumab
medicines.dosage: 10 mg/kg IV (first infusion); 20 mg/kg IV (subsequent infusions) every 3 weeks for 8 doses
medicines.use_case: FDA-approved (2020) for active, moderate-severe Graves' ophthalmopathy. Targets IGF-1R pathway. Reduces proptosis and diplopia.
medicines.mechanism: Monoclonal antibody inhibiting insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor (IGF-1R) — key driver of orbital inflammation in TED

medicines.name: Selenium Supplementation
medicines.use_case: Mild active Graves' ophthalmopathy (EUGOGO European Group recommendation); reduces oxidative stress in orbital tissues
side_effects: Selenosis (garlic breath, hair loss — with chronic excessive intake)

medicines.name: Artificial Tears and Lubricating Eye Drops
medicines.use_case: Corneal protection in all stages of Graves' eye disease; prevents dryness and corneal damage
side_effects: Minimal; blurred vision temporarily with ointments

categories.purpose: Combination therapy to rapidly lower thyroid hormone levels and block its effects in life-threatening thyrotoxic crisis. Always managed in ICU.
categories.note: Thyroid storm requires simultaneous multi-drug approach: Step 1 - block synthesis (PTU/MMI); Step 2 - block release (Lugol's, 1 hour AFTER step 1); Step 3 - block effects (beta-blocker, steroid); Step 4 - supportive care

medicines.name: Full Thyroid Storm Protocol (Summary)
medicines.dosage: PTU 200-250 mg every 4h OR methimazole 20-25 mg every 4h → Lugol's iodine 5 drops every 6h (1h after PTU/MMI) → Propranolol 60-80 mg every 4-6h oral or 1-2 mg IV → Dexamethasone 2 mg every 6h → Treat precipitant (infection, surgery) → Supportive ICU care
medicines.use_case: Life-threatening thyroid storm (Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45)
medicines.monitoring: Continuous cardiac monitoring; ICU level care; aim to reduce temperature, heart rate, and agitation; reassess every 4-6 hours

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet plays a vital supportive role in managing hyperthyroidism. The primary dietary goal is to limit iodine intake (iodine is raw material for thyroid hormone synthesis), support bone health (threatened by accelerated resorption), manage accelerated metabolism with adequate calories and protein, and reduce cardiovascular stress with anti-inflammatory eating patterns.

items.food: Non-iodized salt
items.benefit: Avoids dietary iodine that fuels thyroid hormone overproduction; use only non-iodized salt in cooking

items.food: Fresh fruits (non-iodized): Apples, Bananas, Mangoes, Papaya, Pears, Grapes
items.benefit: Naturally low in iodine; high in vitamins, antioxidants, and fibre; support immune function

items.food: Fresh vegetables: Broccoli, Cabbage, Cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, Kale, Turnips
items.benefit: Goitrogenic vegetables naturally reduce thyroid hormone synthesis (by inhibiting TPO); low-iodine; high in antioxidants
items.frequency: Several servings per week; cooked reduces goitrogenic effect

items.food: Unsalted rice, pasta, oats, and cereals (without iodized salt)
items.benefit: Energy source with low iodine; provides B vitamins for nervous system (stressed by hyperthyroidism)

items.food: Egg whites (avoid yolks on strict low-iodine diet)
items.benefit: High-quality protein without iodine from egg yolk; supports muscle preservation

recommended_foods.category: Calcium and Vitamin D Rich Foods (Bone Protection)

items.food: Fortified plant-based milk (soy, almond, oat) without iodine
items.benefit: Calcium and Vitamin D for bone protection; hyperthyroidism depletes bone calcium via accelerated resorption

items.food: Green leafy vegetables: Spinach, Kale, Bok choy, Collard greens, Methi (fenugreek)
items.benefit: Calcium source (non-dairy); magnesium for muscle function; Vitamin K for bone matrix

items.food: Tofu and edamame (calcium-set tofu)
items.benefit: Calcium-rich plant protein; bone-protective; isoflavones in soy may have mild goitrogenic effect (beneficial in hyperthyroidism)

items.food: Almonds (unsalted)
items.benefit: Calcium, magnesium, and healthy fats; bone and cardiovascular support

items.food: Sunlight exposure (15-20 minutes daily)
items.benefit: Primary source of Vitamin D; essential for calcium absorption and bone health

items.food: Whole grains: Brown rice, Quinoa, Oats, Whole wheat bread
items.benefit: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy for hypermetabolic state; B vitamins; magnesium

items.food: Lean proteins: Chicken breast, Turkey, Lentils, Chickpeas, Beans
items.benefit: Muscle catabolism increased in hyperthyroidism; adequate protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day) prevents muscle loss and supports weight maintenance

items.food: Healthy fats: Avocado, Olive oil, Nuts, Flaxseeds, Chia seeds
items.benefit: Calorie-dense; anti-inflammatory omega-3 fatty acids; support hormone regulation and cardiovascular health

items.food: Starchy vegetables: Sweet potato, Potatoes, Corn, Peas
items.benefit: Additional complex carbohydrate calories; potassium (important for heart rhythm in tachycardia); Vitamin A

items.food: Berries: Blueberries, Strawberries, Raspberries, Blackberries
items.benefit: High antioxidant content (flavonoids, polyphenols); reduce oxidative stress generated by hypermetabolism; anti-inflammatory

items.food: Turmeric with black pepper
items.benefit: Curcumin reduces inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α); may modulate autoimmune response in Graves' disease
items.frequency: Daily in cooking or golden milk

items.food: Ginger
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory, antioxidant; reduces nausea (common GI symptom); may help with anxiety

items.food: Green tea (lightly brewed)
items.benefit: EGCG catechins — antioxidant and anti-inflammatory; low caffeine when brewed lightly; contains fluoride which may mildly inhibit thyroid
items.frequency: 1 cup daily (avoid high intake — caffeine worsens palpitations)

recommended_foods.category: Selenium-Rich Foods (Thyroid and Eye Disease Support)

items.food: Brazil nuts (1-2 per day only)
items.benefit: Richest dietary source of selenium; selenium is essential for thyroid hormone metabolism and antioxidant defense (selenoproteins); clinical evidence supports 200 mcg selenium daily reduces mild Graves' ophthalmopathy
items.frequency: 1-2 Brazil nuts daily (1 nut ≈ 70-90 mcg selenium; do not exceed 400 mcg/day)

items.food: Sunflower seeds, Mushrooms
items.benefit: Selenium and antioxidants; support thyroid antioxidant enzymes (glutathione peroxidase, thioredoxin reductase)

items.food: Dark leafy greens, Pumpkin seeds, Flaxseeds, Lentils
items.benefit: Magnesium helps regulate heart rhythm (reduces palpitations and tachycardia risk); important in hypermetabolic state; magnesium depleted rapidly in hyperthyroidism

items.food: Oats, quinoa, brown rice
items.benefit: Magnesium and potassium; cardiovascular support; nerve and muscle function

foods_to_avoid.reason: Iodine is the primary raw material for thyroid hormone synthesis. Excess iodine directly worsens hyperthyroidism and can trigger thyroid storm (Jod-Basedow effect in some patients).
examples: Seafood: shrimp, crab, lobster, oysters, saltwater fish
Dairy products (contain iodine from feed and udder wash)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Caffeine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, directly worsening the already-elevated heart rate, palpitations, tremors, anxiety, and insomnia caused by hyperthyroidism. Completely avoid during active hyperthyroidism.

Alcohol exacerbates tachycardia, liver stress (especially important as antithyroid drugs can affect liver), dehydration, and cardiovascular complications of hyperthyroidism. Avoid completely during active disease.

Growing evidence links gluten sensitivity/celiac disease with Graves' disease due to shared autoimmune pathways. A gluten-free diet may reduce autoimmune activation in TRAb-positive patients. Discuss with endocrinologist.

foods_to_avoid.food: Soy products (in patients on levothyroxine post-treatment)
foods_to_avoid.reason: Soy isoflavones may interfere with thyroid hormone absorption from levothyroxine. Avoid soy 4 hours before or after taking levothyroxine. Also has mild goitrogenic effect (this may be beneficial during active hyperthyroidism).
Spicy foods increase body heat and sweating, worsening the heat intolerance and hyperhidrosis characteristic of hyperthyroidism. Contribute to discomfort during active disease.
Promote systemic inflammation; displace nutrient-dense food needed to support the hypermetabolic state; can worsen anxiety and mood instability.
Conventional dairy products (milk, cheese, butter) contain significant iodine due to use of iodine-based teat disinfectants and iodine-supplemented animal feed. Limit on low-iodine diet.
Many multivitamins, cough syrups, antiseptics, and amiodarone contain high iodine that worsens hyperthyroidism.

sample_meal_plan.note: This low-iodine, high-calorie, bone-protective meal plan is a general guideline. Individual nutritional needs may vary based on severity of hyperthyroidism, weight, and treatment phase. Consult a registered dietitian and endocrinologist.
sample_meal_plan.early_morning: Warm water with lemon and 1/4 tsp turmeric + 4-5 soaked almonds (unsalted) + 1-2 Brazil nuts (selenium)
sample_meal_plan.breakfast: Oatmeal with blueberries, chia seeds, and almond milk (fortified, non-iodized) OR Vegetable upma with non-iodized salt + 1 cup lightly brewed green tea
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning: 1 banana or papaya OR smoothie with spinach, banana, and almond milk
sample_meal_plan.lunch: Brown rice or quinoa + lentil dal (non-iodized salt) + stir-fried broccoli with garlic and olive oil + tofu cubes OR grilled chicken breast
sample_meal_plan.evening_snack: Unsalted pumpkin seeds + fresh fruit (apple, pear, grapes) OR handful of walnuts with fresh cucumber
sample_meal_plan.dinner: Grilled or baked salmon (small portion — controlled iodine) OR paneer with vegetables + whole wheat chapati (non-iodized salt) + mixed vegetable curry with cauliflower/cabbage
sample_meal_plan.before_bed: Warm calcium-fortified plant milk OR chamomile herbal tea

special_dietary_notes: Follow a low-iodine diet, particularly when preparing for radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy — strict low-iodine diet (LID) required for 1-2 weeks before RAI to enhance radioiodine uptake
Increase caloric intake by 10-15% above normal requirements to compensate for hypermetabolic state and prevent weight loss
Eat small, frequent meals (5-6 per day) to maintain blood sugar, manage GI symptoms, and prevent nausea
Ensure calcium intake of 1000-1200 mg/day and Vitamin D 1500-2000 IU/day throughout treatment to protect bone density
Keep a food diary to identify personal dietary triggers (especially if histamine or food sensitivities suspected)
Adequate protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg body weight daily) to prevent hyperthyroid-related muscle wasting
On levothyroxine replacement post-treatment: take medication 30-60 minutes before breakfast; avoid calcium, iron, soy within 4 hours of dose
Once euthyroid (thyroid function normal after treatment): gradually transition to a balanced healthy diet; iodine restriction less critical

trigger_avoidance: Avoid iodine-containing supplements, kelp tablets, and iodine-rich foods (seaweed, iodized salt) throughout treatment
Stop smoking — smoking significantly worsens Graves' ophthalmopathy and increases the risk of Graves' disease relapse
Avoid stress wherever possible — psychological stress can trigger Graves' disease onset and relapse; stress directly activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis
Inform all physicians about hyperthyroidism before any imaging with contrast dye (iodinated contrast can trigger thyroid storm)
Avoid amiodarone if alternative cardiac drugs exist — amiodarone contains 37% iodine and can precipitate or worsen hyperthyroidism
Avoid high-dose vitamin supplements containing iodine during treatment
Protect eyes if Graves' ophthalmopathy is present — wear UV-protective sunglasses outdoors; use lubricating eye drops regularly; avoid dry environments
Avoid extreme heat exposure (saunas, hot baths, very hot weather) — worsens heat intolerance, tachycardia, and dehydration
Monitor caffeine and stimulant intake — caffeine worsens palpitations and anxiety
Maintain good sleep hygiene — hyperthyroidism causes insomnia; prioritize 7-9 hours of sleep per night

recommended: Light walking (30 minutes daily at comfortable pace once heart rate is controlled with beta-blockers)
Gentle yoga and stretching — low impact; supports stress management and flexibility
Tai chi and qigong — slow, controlled movements; excellent for stress reduction and balance
Swimming (moderate pace) — once thyroid function is improving with treatment
Gentle resistance/strength training with light weights — helps preserve muscle mass lost from hyperthyroid catabolism
avoid_during_active_untreated_hyperthyro: Heavy weight lifting or competitive sports
Marathon running or long-distance endurance events
Contact sports or physically demanding exercise
Exercise in hot or humid environments
precautions: Always check heart rate before exercising — avoid exercise if resting heart rate >100 bpm until controlled
Monitor for palpitations, chest pain, or severe breathlessness during activity — stop and rest immediately
Carry water and rehydrate frequently — sweating and heat intolerance increase dehydration risk
Wear heart rate monitor to avoid overexertion
Resume normal activity only after TSH and heart rate are within normal range under treatment
Consult endocrinologist and cardiologist before starting exercise program if atrial fibrillation diagnosed
physical_activity.note: Exercise is beneficial for bone density, cardiovascular health, and mood — but must be appropriately modified based on disease severity and cardiac status. Resume normal exercise gradually as hyperthyroidism comes under control.

eye_care.description: Graves' ophthalmopathy (Thyroid Eye Disease/TED) requires specific lifestyle adaptations to protect the eyes and prevent vision loss.
measures: Wear high-quality UV-protective sunglasses outdoors — especially important with proptosis
Use preservative-free lubricating eye drops frequently (every 2-4 hours) to prevent corneal drying
Use lubricating eye ointment at night; tape eyelids closed gently if incomplete closure (lagophthalmos)
Elevate head of bed 15-30 degrees at night to reduce periorbital edema
Apply cool compresses to eyes for swelling and discomfort
Avoid smoke and dusty environments — eye irritation worsened in TED
STOP smoking immediately — smoking is the single most important modifiable risk factor for TED severity and progression
Attend regular ophthalmology follow-up — visual acuity, corneal health, and eye pressure monitoring
Avoid RAI therapy if moderate-severe active Graves' ophthalmopathy present (can worsen TED); discuss with doctor

bone_health.description: Chronic hyperthyroidism causes accelerated bone resorption leading to osteopenia and osteoporosis — especially in postmenopausal women and elderly.
measures: Ensure calcium intake 1000-1200 mg/day through diet and supplements
Ensure Vitamin D levels >30 ng/mL (supplement 1000-2000 IU/day)
Weight-bearing exercise (walking, gentle resistance training) stimulates bone formation
DEXA bone density scan at diagnosis, then annually if abnormal
Avoid smoking and alcohol — both independently reduce bone density
Bisphosphonates if DEXA confirms osteoporosis (T-score < -2.5) — under physician supervision
Maintain adequate protein and magnesium intake

mental_health: Seek professional mental health support — anxiety and depression are common in hyperthyroidism and worsen symptoms
Practice mindfulness meditation — reduces stress-induced symptom flares; 10-20 minutes daily
Progressive muscle relaxation — helps counter the muscle tension and tremors from hyperthyroidism
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) — effective for anxiety associated with palpitations and breathlessness
Join thyroid patient support groups (e.g., Thyroid UK, American Thyroid Association patient resources) for emotional support
Communicate with family and employers about condition — explain fatigue, mood changes, and need for schedule adjustments
Limit screen time before bed — exacerbates insomnia already worsened by hyperthyroidism
Practice sleep hygiene — consistent bedtime, cool dark room, avoid caffeine after noon

thyroid_monitoring_plan.note: Unlike asthma which has peak flow zones, hyperthyroidism is monitored through laboratory values (TSH, Free T4, Free T3), symptom assessment, and heart rate. This plan helps patients and caregivers understand when to take action.

green_zone.lab_values: TSH: 0.4-4.0 mIU/L; Free T4: 0.8-1.8 ng/dL; Free T3: 2.3-4.1 pg/mL
green_zone.symptoms: No or minimal symptoms; sleeping well; maintaining weight; no palpitations at rest
green_zone.action: Continue prescribed medications at current dose. Regular follow-up every 3-6 months. Maintain healthy lifestyle and low-iodine diet.

yellow_zone.lab_values: TSH < 0.4 mIU/L or >4.0 mIU/L; Free T4 elevated or suppressed
yellow_zone.symptoms: Returning palpitations, increased tremors, new weight changes, worsening anxiety, heat intolerance, or insomnia
yellow_zone.action: Contact endocrinologist within 1-2 days. Do not self-adjust medications. Review for possible iodine exposure. Blood tests (TSH, Free T4) required urgently. Dose adjustment may be needed.

red_zone.lab_values: Markedly elevated Free T3/T4; Burch-Wartofsky score ≥45
red_zone.heart_rate: Heart rate >140 bpm or new irregular heartbeat (atrial fibrillation)
red_zone.symptoms: High fever >38.5°C, extreme tachycardia, agitation, confusion, delirium, vomiting, jaundice, or collapse
red_zone.action: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY (102 / 112 in India; 911 in USA). Go to nearest hospital emergency room. DO NOT drive yourself. This is a life-threatening medical emergency requiring ICU admission.

complications.description: Life-threatening exacerbation of hyperthyroidism characterized by high fever (>38.5°C), extreme tachycardia (>140 bpm), agitation, delirium, heart failure, and coma. Often precipitated by surgery, infection, trauma, or contrast dye exposure in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism. Mortality 10-30% even with treatment.
complications.prevention: Achieve euthyroid state before surgery; avoid iodinated contrast in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism; prompt treatment of infections

complications.description: Irregular rapid heartbeat affecting 10-15% of hyperthyroid patients (up to 25-40% in elderly). Thyroid hormones directly sensitize the heart to catecholamines. Associated with high risk of stroke (thromboembolism) — anticoagulation required.
complications.note: Cardioversion or rate control with beta-blockers; anticoagulation to prevent stroke

complications.description: Hyperthyroidism causes high-output heart failure by increasing cardiac output beyond the heart's capacity. Presents with breathlessness, peripheral edema, and reduced exercise tolerance.
complications.note: Resolves with treatment of hyperthyroidism; may require temporary heart failure management

complications.description: Chronic hyperthyroidism increases bone resorption via direct effects of thyroid hormones on osteoclasts. Bone mineral density decreases, particularly at the hip and spine, increasing fracture risk in postmenopausal women and elderly.
complications.note: Calcium, Vitamin D, bisphosphonates; DEXA monitoring; exercise

complications.description: Autoimmune inflammatory disease of the orbit occurring in ~25-50% of Graves' disease patients. Ranges from mild lid retraction and dry eyes to severe proptosis, corneal ulceration, compressive optic neuropathy, and permanent vision loss.
complications.note: Stop smoking; selenium supplementation for mild disease; IV methylprednisolone for moderate-severe; teprotumumab (Tepezza) for active disease; orbital decompression surgery if vision threatened

complications.description: Sudden attacks of profound muscle weakness or paralysis, usually in lower limbs. Caused by hyperthyroid-induced hypokalemia (potassium shifts into cells). Predominantly in Asian men with Graves' disease.
complications.severity: Moderate to severe (life-threatening if affects respiratory muscles)
complications.note: IV potassium replacement; beta-blockers; treat hyperthyroidism urgently

complications.description: Hyperthyroidism causes menstrual irregularities (oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea), anovulation, and reduced fertility. In pregnancy, untreated hyperthyroidism causes miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, and neonatal thyrotoxicosis.

Iatrogenic hypothyroidism is the most common outcome after radioactive iodine therapy (~80-90%) or total thyroidectomy. Also occurs with overly aggressive antithyroid drug therapy. Requires lifelong levothyroxine replacement.
complications.severity: Manageable — expected and treated with levothyroxine
complications.note: Annual TSH monitoring; dose adjustment as needed

complications.description: Chronic hyperthyroidism causes anxiety disorders, panic attacks, mood instability, emotional lability, cognitive difficulties, and in severe cases psychosis (thyroid madness). Usually resolves with treatment of hyperthyroidism.
complications.note: Temporary anti-anxiety medications may help; psychiatric referral if severe

complications.description: Progressive weakness of proximal muscles (thighs, shoulders, upper arms) from hypermetabolism-induced protein catabolism. Difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair, lifting arms above head.
complications.note: Resolves with thyroid function control; physical therapy for rehabilitation

key_points: Overt hyperthyroidism in pregnancy requires treatment — untreated disease causes more harm than medications
Propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred in the first trimester (methimazole associated with rare aplasia cutis and choanal atresia in fetus)
Methimazole is preferred from second trimester onwards (PTU carries liver toxicity risk)
Use lowest effective dose of antithyroid drugs — aim to keep Free T4 at upper limit of normal (to avoid fetal hypothyroidism)
Radioactive iodine is ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (damages fetal thyroid)
TRAb (TSH receptor antibodies) cross the placenta — monitor fetus for tachycardia and neonatal Graves' disease
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis (hCG-mediated, first trimester) usually self-limiting — supportive care only
Beta-blockers (propranolol) used cautiously in pregnancy for symptom control — associated with fetal growth restriction with prolonged use
Monitor fetal heart rate and growth at each antenatal visit
All postpartum women with prior thyroid disease should be screened for postpartum thyroiditis at 6-12 weeks postpartum
Graves' disease accounts for >95% of childhood hyperthyroidism
Antithyroid drugs (methimazole) are first-line for children — used for 2-4 years before considering definitive therapy
Radioactive iodine use in children is controversial — may be used in adolescents after careful consideration
Surgical thyroidectomy performed in specialized centers with pediatric surgeons for children not responding to drugs
Growth monitoring essential — hyperthyroidism causes advanced bone age and early growth plate closure
School performance must be monitored — hyperthyroidism causes significant behavioral and cognitive disruption
Psychological support for child and family — chronic disease management is stressful
Neonatal Graves' disease: infants born to mothers with high TRAb may develop transient neonatal hyperthyroidism — requires neonatal endocrinology follow-up

Presents atypically as 'apathetic hyperthyroidism' — absent or blunted classic symptoms (no heat intolerance, no anxiety, no hyperactivity); instead presents with lethargy, depression, cognitive decline, weight loss, and new atrial fibrillation
Cardiac complications more prominent — atrial fibrillation (25-40% of elderly hyperthyroid patients), heart failure, angina
Higher stroke risk from atrial fibrillation — anticoagulation (warfarin or NOAC) required
Radioactive iodine preferred definitive treatment in elderly — surgery higher risk; antithyroid drugs used as bridge
Lower doses of antithyroid drugs due to reduced renal clearance
Bone loss is more severe and fracture risk higher in elderly — DEXA scan mandatory
Drug interactions more common — polypharmacy; beta-blockers carefully titrated to avoid bradycardia and falls
Annual TSH monitoring essential — subclinical hyperthyroidism in elderly still increases AF and bone fracture risk
Less common in men (1:5-10 female-to-male ratio) but often more severe when it occurs
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis more common in Asian men with Graves' disease
Erectile dysfunction and reduced libido common — usually resolves with treatment
Gynecomastia (breast enlargement) may occur due to hormonal imbalance
Men often diagnosed later due to atypical or attributed-to-anxiety presentations
Muscle wasting and exercise intolerance common complaints

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral infections can precipitate thyroid storm or worsen hyperthyroidism; patients on immunosuppressive antithyroid drugs may have reduced immunity; annual flu vaccine strongly recommended

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Single dose; booster at age 65 if given earlier
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Pneumococcal infections are a major precipitant of thyroid storm; bacterial pneumonia can trigger severe thyroid crisis in hyperthyroid patients

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: As per current national guidelines (annual updated booster)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 and its treatments (checkpoint inhibitors) can trigger or worsen thyroiditis; severe COVID-19 illness can precipitate thyroid storm
Graves' disease is associated with increased susceptibility to certain infections; hepatitis B vaccination recommended for all adults per general immunization guidelines
Viral illnesses including chickenpox can trigger thyroid storm; important if patient is on immunosuppressive antithyroid drugs
General adult immunization; pertussis (whooping cough) can complicate respiratory status and trigger thyroid events

when_to_see_doctor: Any new or worsening palpitations, irregular heartbeat, or resting heart rate consistently above 100 bpm
Unexplained weight loss of more than 2-3 kg over 1-2 months despite normal or increased appetite
Noticeable neck swelling (goiter) or any new lump in the neck
Eye changes: bulging, redness, double vision, pain, or any vision changes (possible Graves' ophthalmopathy)
Persistent tremors, anxiety, or insomnia that is worsening despite treatment
Symptoms worsening despite taking antithyroid medications as prescribed
Any fever with sore throat or mouth ulcers while on antithyroid drugs (possible agranulocytosis — medical emergency)
Nausea, jaundice, dark urine, or right upper abdominal pain while on PTU (liver toxicity warning)
Planning pregnancy or if pregnant and on antithyroid medications
Annual follow-up after completing antithyroid drug course to check for relapse
Any time TSH result is outside normal range on home monitoring
If on levothyroxine post-treatment: symptoms of under-replacement (fatigue, cold intolerance) or over-replacement (palpitations, weight loss)
emergency_signs: Extremely rapid or irregular heartbeat (>140 bpm or new onset atrial fibrillation)
High fever above 38.5°C (101.3°F) — especially in a hyperthyroid patient not actively infected
Severe agitation, confusion, delirium, or hallucinations
Sudden severe shortness of breath or chest pain
Profuse sweating with inability to regulate body temperature
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain in a hyperthyroid patient (thyroid storm trigger)
Jaundice (yellow skin or eyes) while on antithyroid medication — liver toxicity emergency
Loss of vision or sudden eye pain (optic nerve compression in Graves' eye disease)
Fever and sore throat on antithyroid drugs — possible agranulocytosis (life-threatening low white cells)

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is hyperthyroidism and how is it different from hypothyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid) means the thyroid gland produces too much thyroid hormone, speeding up body functions — causing weight loss, rapid heart rate, heat intolerance, and anxiety. Hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid) is the opposite — too little hormone, causing weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, and depression. Both require different treatments.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is hyperthyroidism curable?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Hyperthyroidism can be permanently cured with radioactive iodine therapy or thyroidectomy (surgery). These treatments eliminate the overactive thyroid tissue. However, they typically cause permanent hypothyroidism, requiring lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Antithyroid drugs achieve remission in approximately 40-50% of Graves' disease patients after 12-18 months.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Graves' disease and why does it cause eye problems?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Graves' disease is an autoimmune condition where the immune system produces antibodies (TRAb/TSI) that stimulate the thyroid and orbital tissues. The same autoimmune process attacks the tissues behind the eyes, causing inflammation, swelling, and pushing the eyeballs forward (proptosis). About 25-50% of Graves' patients develop thyroid eye disease. Smoking significantly worsens eye disease.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is a thyroid storm and how dangerous is it?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) is a life-threatening medical emergency where thyroid hormone levels become dangerously high, causing extreme tachycardia (>140 bpm), high fever, confusion, delirium, and multi-organ failure. Even with ICU treatment, mortality is 10-30%. It is usually triggered by surgery, serious infection, iodine exposure, or contrast dye in an uncontrolled hyperthyroid patient.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How is hyperthyroidism treated?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Three main treatment options: (1) Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, PTU) — taken daily to block thyroid hormone production; safest for short-term and pregnancy; (2) Radioactive iodine (I-131) — a single oral dose that permanently destroys overactive thyroid tissue; standard definitive treatment in the USA; causes hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine; (3) Thyroidectomy (surgery) — removes the thyroid gland; preferred when drugs fail, goiter is large, or cancer suspected.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are antithyroid drugs safe?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, antithyroid drugs (methimazole and PTU) are safe when used as prescribed under medical supervision. The rare but serious risk is agranulocytosis (dangerous drop in white blood cells, <0.5% risk). Patients must stop medication immediately and seek emergency care if they develop fever or sore throat. PTU carries a small risk of severe liver damage — report any jaundice or abdominal pain immediately.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can hyperthyroidism affect my heart?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Thyroid hormones directly increase heart rate and sensitize the heart to adrenaline. This causes persistent resting tachycardia, palpitations, and in 10-15% of cases (higher in elderly), atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm that significantly increases stroke risk. Severe or prolonged hyperthyroidism can cause high-output heart failure. These cardiovascular complications are reversible with treatment of hyperthyroidism.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is radioactive iodine safe?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Radioactive iodine (I-131) has been safely used for over 75 years. The radiation targets only thyroid tissue and does not meaningfully affect other organs. It does not increase cancer risk in adults. Patients need to observe some radiation safety precautions for a few days after treatment. It is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can hyperthyroidism affect my bones?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Excess thyroid hormones accelerate bone resorption, causing decreased bone density (osteopenia/osteoporosis) over time, especially in postmenopausal women and elderly. Regular DEXA scans, adequate calcium (1000-1200 mg/day) and Vitamin D intake, weight-bearing exercise, and avoiding smoking are essential bone-protective strategies.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can I get pregnant with hyperthyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes, but hyperthyroidism requires careful management during pregnancy. Untreated hyperthyroidism causes miscarriage, preterm birth, preeclampsia, and fetal thyroid problems. PTU is the preferred antithyroid drug in the first trimester. Radioactive iodine is completely contraindicated. Work closely with your endocrinologist and obstetrician from preconception onwards.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I avoid with hyperthyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Avoid: (1) Iodine-rich foods — seaweed, kelp, seafood, iodized salt (iodine fuels hormone overproduction); (2) Caffeine — worsens palpitations, anxiety, and insomnia; (3) Alcohol — worsens cardiovascular symptoms and liver stress from medications; (4) Spicy foods — worsens heat intolerance; (5) Soy in patients on levothyroxine — interferes with absorption.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What lifestyle changes help manage hyperthyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Key lifestyle measures: (1) Stop smoking — most critical for Graves' ophthalmopathy; (2) Avoid iodine-rich foods; (3) Reduce caffeine; (4) Manage stress (yoga, meditation, CBT); (5) Follow a bone-protective diet (calcium, Vitamin D); (6) Avoid intense exercise during active disease; (7) Wear UV sunglasses for eye protection; (8) Get regular thyroid blood tests; (9) Inform all doctors about your condition and medications.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does hyperthyroidism cause weight loss even with eating more?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. This is one of the hallmark signs of hyperthyroidism. Excess thyroid hormones dramatically accelerate the basal metabolic rate (the body's engine), burning far more calories than normal. Despite increased appetite and eating more, the body loses weight — fat stores and eventually muscle tissue are used for fuel. Weight typically normalizes once thyroid function is controlled with treatment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can hyperthyroidism cause anxiety and mood problems?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes. Excess thyroid hormones amplify the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) nervous system, causing anxiety, nervousness, irritability, emotional lability, racing thoughts, panic attacks, and difficulty concentrating. These are direct biochemical effects of thyroid hormone on the brain. These psychiatric symptoms typically resolve once thyroid function is normalized. If severe, temporary anti-anxiety medication and CBT can help.
